title: Gauss Lab: Symmetry at Work
summary: Choose the right Gaussian surface and use symmetry to find the field of a wire, a sheet, plates and a charged shell.
subject: physics
concepts: Choosing a Gaussian surface by symmetry
Field of an infinite line charge
Field of a sheet and of parallel plates
Field of a charged spherical shell
learningOutcome: The student can pick the Gaussian surface that fits a charge distribution, and find the field of a long wire, a large sheet, parallel plates and a uniformly charged shell.

levels.title: Pick the surface
levels.adds: Baseline: match the Gaussian surface to the symmetry: sphere, cylinder or pillbox.
hints: The field must be perpendicular to the surface and the same size everywhere on it (or parallel to it, with no flux).
A point charge and a sphere of charge have spherical symmetry.
A long wire has cylindrical symmetry; a large flat sheet has planar symmetry.

levels.title: The long wire
levels.adds: New idea: the field of a line charge is E = λ/2πε₀r, falling as 1/r (Ex 1.22).
hints: Use a coaxial cylinder: E × 2πrl = λl/ε₀.
So E = λ/(2πε₀r) = 2kλ/r. Convert the distance to metres.

levels.title: Sheets and plates
levels.adds: New idea: a sheet gives σ/2ε₀ at any distance; opposite plates give σ/ε₀ between and zero outside (Ex 1.23).
hints: A pillbox through the sheet gives 2EA = σA/ε₀, so E = σ/2ε₀.
This field does not depend on the distance from the sheet.
Two opposite plates: the fields add between them and cancel outside.

levels.title: Inside or outside the shell
levels.adds: New idea: a uniformly charged shell has no field inside and acts like a point charge outside (Example 1.12).
hints: Compare the probe’s distance with the shell’s radius first.
A Gaussian sphere inside the shell encloses no charge, so E = 0 there.
Outside, E = kq/r², outward for positive q and inward for negative q.

levels.title: Find the charge
levels.adds: Harder: work backwards from the field outside a sphere to its charge, with the sign (Ex 1.20).
hints: Outside the sphere E = kq/r², so |q| = E r²/k.
The direction of the field gives the sign: outward means positive, inward means negative.
The radius of the sphere does not enter, only the distance from the centre.

misconceptions: The field of a long wire falls as 1/r²
The field of a large sheet weakens with distance
There is a field inside a uniformly charged shell
Any closed surface makes Gauss’s law easy to use
